newsitem.title: USA: Stratosphere bondholders face more pain.
newsitem.headline: Stratosphere bondholders face more pain.

text.p: Plans for financial recovery at Stratosphere Corp became more questionable on Thursday after Grand Casinos said inadequate cash flows may prompt it to withdraw its support, analysts said.
And holders of Stratophere's first mortgage notes should expect to take the brunt of pains associated with any revised restructuring proposal, they added.

"(Bondholders) either accept a significant haircut of principle or they risk that Grand walks away completely and then be stuck with a casino that is eventually going to run out of cash and is going to close," said Steve Patricola, high-yield gaming analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston.

Grand Casino on Wednesday evening said it may end its participation in the reorganization plan because it did not expect Stratosphere to match a minimum monthly average cash flow requirement of $2.267 million. It added that it would not consider a waiver of that requirement but that it is prepared to participate in alternative plans of reorganization.
Stratosphere's cash flow improved in March, but its average cash flow for the six-months ended March 30 reached only $1.727 million.

Stratosphere and 42 percent owner Grand Casinos agreed on a Chapter 11 bankruptcy restructuring plan on January 6. Terms included a coupon cut for bondholders and a rights offering meant to raise $75 million.

Steve Ruggiero, director of securities research at Chase Securities Inc, said the bondholders will likely face a new restructuring plan that would force them to accept equity for their current investments. But perhaps more importantly, the exit of Grand will further jeopardize construction of the second hotel tower that is seen as a keystone of success.

"(Grand) is going to have to put something even if they walk away, but bondholders are the ones with the biggest challenge," Ruggiero said. "They won't get a new hotel out of this if Grand steps away and my precept has always been that cash flow is not sustainable for this entity unless you put in a new hotel..."

Grand's statement just three months from enactment of the plan that would provide for cash to complete the casino is yet another negative harbinger for the project, said Richard Byrne, manager of global high-yield credit research at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.

Analysts noted "make-well" language in the bonds' indenture that requires Grand to invest $20 million in Stratosphere for three years should earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization fall below a predetermined level.
However, even that cash may fall through.
Grand claimed in a recent 10K filing that there is a legal loophole that would allow them to sidestep that obligation, according to Credit Suisse's Patricola.
Cash flows may increase in the coming months due to seasonal factors, but analysts did not hold much hope that the monthly average for six months through June would meet the prescribed requirement.

Stratosphere debt dropped three points on Thursday to 76 bid, 77 offer from bids seen earlier in the week. That move is far from representative of the bonds' worth, however, given the liklihood of Grand's exit, Patricola said.
"Under any reasonable workout scenario this paper should be trading in the 40s to low-50s," he said.
